posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-score post from a CRO in financial services with multiple ICP prospects engaging — validate the auditability pain as the real blocker, not AI itself, to position Milo's explainability angle without naming it
posts.draft_comment: The ban usually isn't about the AI being wrong — it's that nobody can retrace the steps when it matters. Regulators don't need a perfect answer, they need a defensible one. There's a version of AI-assisted analytics where every figure has a clear lineage you can hand to an auditor without breaking a sweat. Curious whether you see that as a tooling problem or a culture problem in most teams you've encountered?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that the dashboard isn't the product, the confidence is
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never really the problem. It's that finance teams have been burned before — a number looks wrong once in a meeting and they go back to the spreadsheet forever. What you're actually building isn't a BI tool, it's enough trust that someone will stake their reputation on a figure in front of a board. Have you figured out what finally moves that needle for them?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why people don't look' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is just a sign that nobody wanted to make a hard call about what actually matters. The dashboard becomes a political document — everyone's metric has to be in there. What's wild is the 10% usage number, because the 90% who never opened it still had opinions about what it should show.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail is engaging on a post about BI chaos and data ownership — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing with a sharper take on why governance fails before tools do
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't really a Power BI problem — it's what happens when you hand out tools before anyone's agreed on what 'good' looks like. Most orgs skip straight to access and wonder why they end up with three versions of revenue. Democratising data only works if someone's already done the unglamorous work of defining it. Who actually owned that in your org before the licences went out?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as security risk with CEO of 90-person data company engaging — validate the security framing, add the trust-chain insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing shift here matters. Most teams are still treating hallucinated outputs as a QA problem — something to catch before the report goes out. But if the model is the one generating the report, you've already lost the audit trail that makes scrutiny possible in the first place. Who's accountable when the source of truth doesn't have a source?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm naming the vendor-reality gap, with a COO prospect engaging — validate the structural problem with a specific observation, add the real reason it happens
posts.draft_comment: The £200k number stings but it's not even the worst part — the worst part is that everyone nodded along in the demo and genuinely believed it would work. Most BI tools are architected around the person who writes the queries, not the person who needs an answer at 8am before a client call. So 'self-service' ends up meaning 'self-service if you already know SQL'. Curious whether your client ever got a straight answer on that from the vendor before they signed.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' wall — validate the cultural diagnosis but add the layer that culture and tooling are tangled, not separate
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is real, but I'd push back slightly on separating culture from tooling — because usually the reason three teams apply three different filters is that nobody agreed on definitions upstream, and the tool never forced that conversation. So it's less 'AI won't fix this' and more 'nothing fixes this until someone owns the metric, not just the dashboard.' Did the CFO leave that meeting wanting a process owner, or just better numbers next quarter?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption failure mode (no one knows what to ask) — validate the 'blank page problem' and add the shadow AI angle as a signal worth paying attention to
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is everywhere right now, and I think you've named the actual reason better than most — it's not adoption friction, it's that people don't know what good looks like with a general-purpose tool. Shadow AI is the tell though. When someone's sneaking ChatGPT on their phone to do their job, that's not a compliance problem, that's a product-fit problem. What were the 12% actually using it for?
